title: MoE Circuit Tracer
tagline: Trains two identical MoE transformers with different load balancing and asks which one still knows what it's looking at.
description: Mixture of experts models are supposed to specialise: anatomy tokens to one expert, code tokens to another. I wanted to know whether the load balancing mechanism itself gets in the way of that. So I trained two identical DeepSeekMoE style transformers (298M parameters, 32 routed experts plus 2 shared, top 4 selection) on WikiText 2 for 10 epochs, differing only in balancing strategy: the auxiliary loss free bias approach from DeepSeek V3 versus a standard auxiliary loss penalty. Then I probed routing across 57 MMLU subjects and measured per subject routing entropy as a proxy for whether the router carries any information about its input.

The result is a genuine tension. Auxiliary loss free balancing does its job perfectly, all 32 experts within 0.1% of uniform by epoch 2, but its routing entropy sits at 98.5% of the theoretical maximum. The router is essentially rolling dice whether you show it anatomy or abstract algebra. The auxiliary loss model never balances properly, yet it preserves a weak structural signal in 55 of 57 subjects. The cause is scale: at 298M parameters the accumulated bias terms simply overwhelm the still weak semantic differences between experts. This is a small scale finding and I say so in the paper; a replication at 1B or larger is the planned next step once compute allows.

paper.title: Load Balancing Mechanisms in Mixture-of-Experts Transformers Suppress Routing Informativeness at Small Scale: An Empirical Circuit-Tracing Study
paper.abstract: Two otherwise identical DeepSeekMoE style transformers (298M parameters, 32 routed plus 2 shared experts, top 4 selection) are trained on WikiText 2, one with auxiliary loss free balancing and one with a standard auxiliary loss penalty. Both reach equivalent language quality (final loss 2.793 vs 2.758). Auxiliary loss free balancing achieves near perfect load distribution but routing entropy of 98.5% of the theoretical maximum, meaning the routing distribution is nearly uniform regardless of input domain. The auxiliary loss model fails to fully balance but produces lower per subject entropy in 55 of 57 MMLU subjects. We attribute the effect to a scale mismatch between accumulated bias terms and expert semantic differentiation, and discuss implications for balancing design at small scale.
